# Statement Convention

Two habits make a function readable top to bottom instead of inside out: each statement does one thing, and the success case comes first. Without them a reader has to evaluate a nested expression in their head to find out what a line returns, and has to hold a negation in mind for the rest of the function to work out which branch is the normal one.

## Scope

Applies to every hand-written `.ts` / `.tsx` / `.js` source file.

Does **not** apply to generated output (codegen, tool-emitted `*.d.ts`, build directories), database migrations, or third-party shims copied verbatim.

## One Statement, One Job

Separate _reading a value_ from _acting on it_. Each statement does one thing; a blank line sits between the read and the action. Never bury `??`, a ternary, or an optional chain inside the argument of `throw`, `return`, or a function call — destructure with a default first, then act.

```ts
// CORRECT — read with a default, blank line, then act
if (errors) {
  const { message = 'Failed to fetch account' } = errors;

  throw new UpstreamError(message);
}

// WRONG — read and act squeezed into one expression
if (errors) {
  throw new UpstreamError(errors.message ?? 'Failed to fetch account');
}
```

The named local is the point: it gives the value a name a reader can check against the type, and it gives a debugger somewhere to stop.

## Happy Path First, Positive Conditions

Write conditions in the affirmative (`if (token)`, not `if (!token)`). The success branch comes first; the `throw` or `return null` is the last statement of the function. Do not write a negated guard followed by the happy path.

```ts
// CORRECT — affirmative check, success on top, throw at the end
const token = readAccessToken(data);

if (token) {
  return token;
}

throw new UpstreamError('No access token returned');

// CORRECT — same shape when the fallback is null
const account = readAccount(data);

if (account) {
  return { id: account.id, email: account.email ?? null, name: account.name };
}

return null;

// WRONG — negated guard, throw in the middle, happy path pushed to the bottom
const token = data?.accessTokenCreate?.accessToken;

if (!token) {
  throw new UpstreamError('No access token returned');
}

return token;
```

Reading the function then answers the question people actually arrive with — *what does this return when it works* — in the first branch, and leaves the failure as the last line rather than something to scroll past.

## NEVER Do

- Bury `??`, a ternary, or an optional chain inside the argument of `throw`, `return`, or a call — destructure with a default first, act on the next statement.
- Write a negated guard (`if (!x) { throw … } return x;`) — check in the affirmative, happy path first, `throw` / `return null` last.
